appraisal_events.evidence: Le célèbre écrivain vient spontanément près d’elle, « le charme qu’elle avait, son tact, sa simplicité la lui faisant considérer comme une femme d’esprit » ; elle réunit « certains hommes d’élite » que des « altesses curieuses » veulent rencontrer, et, tirant d’un « tuf plus solide », place « quelque citation de Victor Hugo ou de Lamartine » qui « ne manquait pas de surprendre et de charmer », ou donne « quelque conseil sagace » à un auteur dramatique académicien.
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage establishes the duchess as the magnetic center of a salon that distinguished men, wives excluded, are honored to enter, and closes by crediting her with real cultivation and judgment beneath the frivolity. Both the social pull and the closing demonstration of discernment are narrated as fact rather than as someone else's flattery.

appraisal_events.evidence: Le duc explique la « singulière maladie de la duchesse de ne pouvoir fréquenter des femmes » presque « par ordonnance du médecin » ; les épouses écartées soupçonnent jalousie ou « passé scandaleux » ; et l’on se quitte « sans avoir dit un mot de la poésie », ces repas ayant « quelque chose de fort mélancolique ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator ironizes the rule the duchess lives by: her exclusion of other women is dressed up as an illness by her husband and read as jealousy or scandal by the excluded wives, while the vaunted intellectual salon turns out to talk only of eggs and cards. Her prestige is shown to rest on a decorum that is empty and faintly sad.

status_effects.explanation: Locally she is shown reigning over a court of eminent men and desirable guests, able to exclude wives at will and to make attendance a duty for a celebrated writer.

The narrator's irony lowers how she comes off personally: her intellectual reputation is deflated into small talk and her social rule into a fabricated malady, though the closing praise keeps the fall modest.

He is the mouthpiece of the ridiculous medical alibi for his wife's exclusion of women, and the coda has Mme de Villeparisis speak of him with irritation over the queen-of-Sweden prank; he is the one figure the passage lets others openly resent.

ambiguities: The narrative stance on the duchess is layered rather than single: the catalogue of eminent guests is reported in the salon's own idiom and immediately undercut, so the elevation and the ironization run through the same sentences; the closing praise of her Hugo citations and sagacious advice is taken here as narrator-endorsed correction, but it could also be read as one more report of the milieu's self-image.

The evaluator of the harshest readings of the duchess (jealousy, a scandalous past) is the collective voice of the excluded wives, not the narrator, so that discredit is reported rather than affirmed; only the melancholy of the silent meals is clearly the narrator's own judgment.
